data.title: Milium / colloid milium — viva
data.summary: Benign tumours & cysts · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Milium / colloid milium** (Benign tumours & cysts)_

**Q1. What are milia?**
- Small (1–2 mm), superficial, white-yellow, keratin-filled epidermoid cysts (arising from vellus hair follicles or eccrine ducts) — very common on face (eyelids, cheeks, nose) of all ages, especially newborns (~40–50%)

**Q2. Classify milia and explain their clinical features (PYQ).**
- Primary: congenital/neonatal (face, palate — Epstein pearls; gingiva — Bohn's nodules; resolve in weeks), benign primary milia in children/adults (eyelids, cheeks), milia en plaque (cluster on erythematous plaque — retroauricular/eyelid), multiple eruptive milia, nodular grouped milia, genodermatoses (Bazex–Dupré–Christol, Rombo, Gorlin, oro-facial-digital syndrome type I, Marie–Unna hypotrichosis, pachyonychia congenita)
- Secondary: after blistering diseases (EB dystrophica, porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid, EBA), trauma, burns, dermabrasion, laser resurfacing, radiotherapy, potent topical steroids (atrophy), drugs (cyclosporine, penicillamine)

**Q3. Histopathology of milia.**
- Small epidermoid cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with granular layer, containing laminated keratin

**Q4. Treatment of milia.**
- Neonatal: self-resolve — no treatment
- Extraction/de-roofing with a sterile needle or No.11 blade and expression; electrodesiccation, CO2 laser; topical retinoids for multiple; minocycline for milia en plaque

**Q5. Add a note on colloid milium (PYQ).**
- Rare degenerative condition with deposition of homogeneous eosinophilic 'colloid' material in the papillary dermis giving translucent, yellowish-brown or amber, dome-shaped papules that ooze gelatinous material on puncture
- Types: adult colloid milium (commonest — sun-exposed face, dorsa of hands, neck in middle-aged outdoor workers; chronic UV, petroleum/hydroquinone exposure; derived from elastic fibres/solar elastosis), juvenile colloid milium (before puberty; derived from keratinocytes — keratin; may be familial; associated with ligneous conjunctivitis), nodular colloid degeneration (single nodule, face/trunk), pigmented colloid milium (hydroquinone-related, ochronosis-like)
- Histology: fissured homogeneous eosinophilic material in papillary dermis with clefts, grenz zone; stains weakly with Congo red/PAS (may mimic amyloid); juvenile type keratin-positive
- Differential: lichen/nodular amyloidosis, syringomas, sebaceous hyperplasia, lipoid proteinosis, milia, hydrocystomas, xanthomas, molluscum
- Treatment: photoprotection; dermabrasion, cryotherapy, CO2/Er:YAG/fractional lasers, diathermy, curettage — recurrences common

**Q6. What are the types of colloid milium?**
- Adult type (commonest): sun-exposed face/dorsa of hands, middle-aged men with heavy sun exposure or petroleum/hydroquinone exposure — degenerated elastic fibres (elastotic)
- Juvenile (childhood, before puberty — keratinocyte-derived, amyloid-like, familial/ligneous conjunctivitis association), nodular colloid degeneration (single large nodule), pigmented colloid milium (hydroquinone-related ochronosis-like)

**Q7. Histopathology of colloid milium.**
- Fissured homogeneous pale eosinophilic colloid masses in the papillary dermis with clefts, separated from the epidermis by a thin grenz zone; adult type — elastic origin; juvenile — derived from keratinocytes (keratin positive); Congo red may be weakly positive

**Q8. What is milia en plaque?**
- Multiple milia grouped on an erythematous oedematous plaque, usually behind the ears/eyelids — associated with DLE, lichen planopilaris, pseudoxanthoma elasticum; treated by extraction, retinoids, minocycline, surgery

**Q9. Which conditions cause secondary milia?**
- Subepidermal blistering diseases healing with milia — epidermolysis bullosa (dystrophic), porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid, EBA, bullous LP; after dermabrasion, laser resurfacing, burns, potent topical steroids, radiotherapy

## Quick spotter facts
- Tiny white keratin cysts on eyelids — milia
- Translucent amber papules on sun-exposed face oozing gel — colloid milium

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cysts; colloid milium). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
